issues.legal_issue: After one coparcener has separated and received a partitioned share, neither continued jointness nor separation among the remaining coparceners is presumed, and the party claiming a particular family status bears the burden of proving it.
material_facts: It was admitted that one member of the family had separated and received a share of the joint property partitioned for him.
The parties disputed whether the deceased member and another coparcener remained joint at the deceased member’s death.
issues.conclusion: There was no presumption either that the remaining coparceners continued joint or that all had separated. Their status had to be determined from the evidence, and the party asserting the state of affairs on which relief depended bore the burden of proof.
issues.legal_principle: The general presumption that a Hindu family is joint does not determine the status of the remaining coparceners once one coparcener is admitted to have separated and received a partitioned share. The question is one of fact, determined from evidence of the parties’ intention; the party asserting the relevant state of affairs to obtain relief bears the burden. The Court relied on Bal Krishna v. Ram Krishna, Palaniammal v. Muthuvenkatachala, and Balabux Ladhuram v. Rukhmabai.

predicates.family_status_disputed: The parties to a dispute over family property assert different accounts of whether family members remained joint or became separate.
predicates.one_coparcener_separated_with_partitione: A member of the family separated from the others and received a share of family property set apart for that member.

issues.definition: When family status is disputed after one coparcener has separated with a partitioned share, the party seeking relief on the basis of a particular status must prove that status.

issues.legal_issue: After coparceners have separated, living together, conducting business jointly, or dealing with property jointly does not by itself restore their status as coparceners without a reunion.
material_facts: The evidence established an earlier separation among the relevant family members.
After that separation, two members lived together, conducted business jointly, and acquired or dealt with property in both their names.
The opposing party did not claim that the separated members had reunited.
issues.conclusion: The later joint living, business, and property dealings did not restore coparcenary status or give rise to survivorship rights; they could at most create a tenancy in common.
issues.legal_principle: Except in the case of reunion, separated coparceners do not regain coparcenary status under Mitakshara law merely by living together or acting jointly in business or property matters. Such dealings may establish a tenancy in common but do not establish a joint tenancy carrying a right of survivorship.

rule.if: coparcenary_status_disputed and prior_separation and later_joint_dealings and not reunion_asserted

predicates.coparcenary_status_disputed: The parties dispute whether persons holding or dealing with family property have coparcenary status.
predicates.prior_separation: The persons in dispute had previously separated from the family.
predicates.later_joint_dealings: After separating, the persons lived together, conducted business together, or dealt with property jointly.
predicates.reunion_asserted: A party claims that the separated persons later reunited.

issues.definition: Where a prior separation is established and no reunion is claimed, subsequent joint living, business, or property dealings alone do not restore coparcenary status.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased person’s statement against their proprietary interest that they were separated from a joint family is relevant, and a connected assertion that the other coparceners were also separated may be admitted as part of the same statement.
material_facts: A deceased family member stated in an old mortgage document that he had separated from the other family members and that the family properties had been partitioned among them.
The document also stated that the other coparceners were separated from one another.
The statements were made before the dispute arose and were connected with the declarant’s account of his own separation and lack of further interest in the family property.
issues.conclusion: The statements were admissible under section 32(3) of the Evidence Act, including the connected assertion of separation among the other coparceners.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 32(3) of the Evidence Act, a deceased person’s statement against their own interest is relevant. The admissible statement is not limited to the precise fact directly against interest; connected matters involved in and knit up with that statement may also be admitted. The Court relied on Smith v. Blakey and Wigmore on Evidence, article 1465.

rule.if: evidence_admissibility_disputed and declarant_is_dead and statement_is_against_declarants_interest and connected_family_separation_assertion

predicates.evidence_admissibility_disputed: A party disputes whether a statement may be considered as evidence in a proceeding.
predicates.declarant_is_dead: The person who made the statement has died.
predicates.statement_is_against_declarants_interest: The declarant stated facts that were against the declarant’s own proprietary interest.
predicates.connected_family_separation_assertion: The statement also asserted a broader family separation connected with the declarant’s own separation.

issues.definition: A deceased declarant’s statement against their own interest may include connected assertions about family separation as relevant evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The use of the expression “joint family” in a document does not necessarily establish that the family had the legal status and incidents of a joint Hindu family.
material_facts: Some documents described the relevant relatives as a joint family while recording joint business, claims, or dealings.
The documents arose from business and property transactions and did not consistently show that the parties held property as a Mitakshara coparcenary.
Other evidence showed separate interests and equal shares in certain properties.
issues.conclusion: The expression “joint family” in those documents did not necessarily establish a legally joint Hindu family.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “joint family” can be used in either a legal or a loose sense. Its presence in a document, considered in its context, does not by itself prove a joint Hindu family with all its legal incidents.

predicates.family_status_evidence_case: A dispute requires the court to determine whether relatives had the legal status of a joint family.
predicates.document_uses_joint_family_expression: A document describes relatives or their dealings using the expression “joint family.”

issues.definition: In a dispute about legal family status, use of the expression “joint family” in a document alone does not establish that status.

issues.legal_issue: Where contemporaneous evidence establishes separation before a family member’s death and reunion is not claimed, later joint business and property dealings do not make that member’s interest pass by survivorship.
material_facts: Old mortgage documents recorded that the family members had separated and that property had been partitioned among them.
Other documents supported the inference that the deceased member and the surviving coparcener held separate interests before later conducting business together.
The deceased member and the surviving coparcener later conducted business jointly and acquired or dealt with property in both names.
The defendants did not claim a later reunion.
issues.conclusion: The deceased member died separate from the surviving coparcener, so the surviving coparcener did not acquire the deceased member’s property by survivorship; the plaintiff was entitled to succeed on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Separation is a question of fact assessed from the evidence of the parties’ intention. Once separation is established, subsequent joint conduct does not restore coparcenary status absent reunion. A separated member’s interest does not pass to another by survivorship merely because they later lived or acted jointly. The Court applied the principles in Bal Krishna v. Ram Krishna, Palaniammal v. Muthuvenkatachala, and Balabux Ladhuram v. Rukhmabai.

rule.if: succession_dispute_over_family_property and contemporaneous_separation_documents and later_joint_dealings and not reunion_asserted

predicates.succession_dispute_over_family_property: A proceeding concerns competing claims to property after a family member’s death.
predicates.contemporaneous_separation_documents: Documents made before the dispute recorded that family members had separated or that their property had been divided.
predicates.later_joint_dealings: After the recorded separation, family members lived together, conducted business together, or acquired or dealt with property jointly.
predicates.reunion_asserted: A party claims that family members who had separated later reunited.

issues.definition: In a succession dispute, where pre-dispute documents establish separation and no reunion is claimed, later joint dealings do not cause the deceased member’s interest to pass by survivorship.

issues.legal_issue: A decree granting possession and mesne profits must not stand without determination of the disputed properties recoverable and the mesne profits payable.
material_facts: The defendants disputed the existence, ownership, and recoverability of some properties claimed in the suit and asserted that some claims could not be recovered in full.
The trial court had left those property questions undecided after dismissing the suit.
The plaintiff also claimed past and future mesne profits, but the appellate court did not determine the amount or basis for them before granting the requested decree.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the deceased member died separate was affirmed, but the case was remanded for determination of the properties recoverable and the mesne profits, with the option to remit those matters for findings.
issues.legal_principle: A decree for possession must be based on a determination of which disputed properties the plaintiff may recover, and a claim for mesne profits requires determination of the applicable amount or basis. Where the appellate court grants relief without deciding those matters, the case must be remanded for their determination.

rule.if: appeal_from_property_decree and claimed_properties_are_disputed and mesne_profits_are_claimed and appellate_court_did_not_determine_those_matters

predicates.appeal_from_property_decree: A party appeals from a decree granting relief concerning possession of property.
predicates.claimed_properties_are_disputed: The parties dispute which of the properties claimed may be recovered by the person seeking relief.
predicates.mesne_profits_are_claimed: The person seeking relief claims mesne profits for past or future use of property.
predicates.appellate_court_did_not_determine_those_: The appellate court granted relief without deciding which properties were recoverable or determining the mesne profits.

issues.definition: When an appellate court grants a property decree without resolving disputes about the recoverable properties and claimed mesne profits, the case must be remanded for those determinations.
